guide.title: Unit 1: The Global Tapestry: review guide
guide.intro: Between about 1200 and 1450, states in every region drew on older traditions to govern, tax, and justify their power. This unit surveys East Asia, Dar al-Islam, South and Southeast Asia, the Americas, Africa, and Europe, and practices comparing how states were built and held together.

sections.title: East Asia and Dar al-Islam
body: Song China (960–1279) governed through a large bureaucracy staffed by officials who passed civil service examinations on Confucian texts. Neo-Confucianism blended Confucian ethics with Buddhist and Daoist ideas and reinforced family and gender hierarchies. Fast-ripening Champa rice, the Grand Canal, and paper money supported population growth and commercial expansion.

In Dar al-Islam, the Abbasid caliphate weakened and new Turkic Muslim states (the Seljuks, the Mamluks of Egypt, and the Delhi Sultanate) took power. Islam spread through merchants and Sufi teachers as well as conquest, and scholars preserved and extended Greek, Persian, and Indian learning in mathematics, astronomy, and medicine.
points: Belief systems (Confucianism, Buddhism, Islam, Christianity) shaped how rulers justified authority.
Tie each state to how it recruited officials and raised revenue.

sections.title: South and Southeast Asia, the Americas, and Africa
body: In South Asia the Delhi Sultanate ruled a largely Hindu population, while Hindu kingdoms such as Vijayanagara persisted in the south; Hinduism and Buddhism shaped Southeast Asian states such as the Khmer Empire. Sea-based states such as Srivijaya grew rich by controlling trade straits.

In the Americas, the Mexica (Aztec) state collected tribute from conquered city-states, and the Inca governed through a road network and the mit'a, a system of required labor for the state. In Africa, Mali grew wealthy from trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt; Great Zimbabwe traded with the Swahili coast; and Christian Ethiopia built rock-cut churches at Lalibela.
points: Tribute, labor obligations, and trade taxes were different ways of funding a state.
Many African and Asian rulers adopted Islam while keeping local traditions.

sections.title: Europe and comparing states
body: Europe was politically decentralized. Under feudalism, lords exchanged land for military service, and under manorialism serfs worked a lord's land in return for protection. The Roman Catholic Church gave a shared religious framework across many small states, while monarchs in England and France gradually strengthened royal power.

Comparison questions ask for similarities and differences. For example, Song China's examination-based bureaucracy was more centralized than Europe's feudal arrangements, while Mali and the Inca both built large states by controlling key resources (trade goods or labor).
points: A good comparison names a specific similarity or difference and explains it.
The Black Death (1347–1351) caused labor shortages that weakened serfdom in western Europe.

example.prompt: Compare how the Inca state and Song China obtained the labor and revenue they needed.
example.solution: The Inca required households to provide labor service (mit'a) on roads, farms, and armies, while Song China relied on taxes collected by an examination-trained bureaucracy and on a growing commercial economy. Both were centralized, but the Inca drew directly on labor and the Song on taxes and trade.

misconceptions: Merchants, Sufi teachers, and scholars spread Islam widely through trade and teaching.
Power was divided among lords; monarchies centralized only gradually.
“The Aztec and Inca states governed in the same way.”
The Mexica relied on tribute from conquered peoples; the Inca on labor service and roads.
“Civil service exams meant anyone could easily become an official.”
Exams opened some mobility, but preparing for them required wealth and years of study.

passages.title: Source A: An interpretation of Song China, 960–1279
text: “The Song dynasty ruled through scholar-officials rather than hereditary nobles. Men who passed demanding civil service examinations on the Confucian classics staffed a bureaucracy that reached down to the counties. Neo-Confucian thinkers taught that a stable society depended on proper relationships: subjects to rulers, children to parents, wives to husbands. Elite families increasingly bound the feet of their daughters, a practice that limited women's mobility. Meanwhile the economy boomed. Champa rice, a fast-ripening variety brought from Vietnam, allowed two harvests a year in some regions, and the population grew rapidly. The Grand Canal carried grain north, and the state issued paper money to keep up with trade.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.

passages.title: Source B: An interpretation of Dar al-Islam, c. 1200–1450
text: “By 1200 the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad held little real power, and the Mongols destroyed the city in 1258. Yet Islamic societies did not collapse. Turkic Muslim rulers, among them the Seljuks, the Mamluks of Egypt, and the sultans of Delhi, built new states and often defended Sunni Islam. Islam continued to spread, carried less by armies than by merchants and Sufi teachers who adapted their message to local customs. In cities from Cairo to Samarkand, scholars translated and preserved Greek, Persian, and Indian works and added to them. Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's observatory produced astronomical tables used for centuries.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of states in the Americas and Africa
text: “In the Valley of Mexico, the Mexica built their capital, Tenochtitlan, on an island in a lake and demanded tribute in food, cloth, and captives from the city-states they conquered. Farther south, the Inca governed millions in the Andes. Rather than tribute in goods, the Inca required the mit'a, a set period of labor service on roads, terraces, and in the army, and they connected the empire with thousands of miles of roads. In West Africa, the empire of Mali grew rich by taxing the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt. When Mansa Musa traveled to Mecca in 1324, the gold he spent in Cairo was remembered for years.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of Europe, c. 1200–1450
text: “Western Europe in 1200 was a patchwork of kingdoms, duchies, and city-states. Lords granted land to vassals in exchange for military service, and on manors serfs farmed the lord's fields in return for protection and the right to work their own plots. What held this divided world together was the Roman Catholic Church, whose bishops, monasteries, and courts reached into every region. Kings in England and France slowly built stronger royal governments. Then, from 1347 to 1351, the Black Death killed perhaps a third of Europe's people. Surviving peasants found that their labor was suddenly scarce, and many demanded better terms.”

questions.prompt: According to Source A, the Song state chose most of its officials through
choices: civil service examinations on Confucian texts
elections held in each county
inheritance of office within the great noble families
sale of offices to wealthy merchants
questions.explanation: The source says “men who passed demanding civil service examinations on the Confucian classics staffed a bureaucracy.”
choiceExplanations: Song China did not elect officials.
The source contrasts scholar-officials with hereditary nobles.
The source describes examinations, not the sale of office.

questions.prompt: The source's description of Neo-Confucianism best supports which conclusion?
choices: It rejected the idea that rulers deserved obedience.
It replaced the examination system with offices inherited within the leading families.
It encouraged women to take civil service examinations.
It reinforced hierarchical relationships, including women's subordination to men.
questions.explanation: Neo-Confucian thought stressed proper hierarchy (subjects to rulers, wives to husbands), and the source links this to restrictive practices such as foot-binding.
choiceExplanations: It taught obedience to rulers.
The examinations continued under the Song.
Women could not take the examinations.

questions.prompt: Compared with states in western Europe in the same period, the Song state described in Source A was distinctive mainly in its
choices: centralized bureaucracy of officials selected by examination
reliance on a single universal church to unite many separate kingdoms
use of serfs bound to manors
lack of any commercial economy
questions.explanation: Song China was governed by an examination-trained bureaucracy, while western Europe was decentralized, with power divided among lords and the Church as a unifying institution.
choiceExplanations: The Catholic Church played that role in Europe, not in Song China.
Manorial serfdom describes Europe, not Song China.
The Song economy was highly commercial.

came under Song Chinese control
passed to new Turkic Muslim states
was taken over by European crusaders

choiceExplanations: The Byzantines did not regain these lands.
Song China never ruled Dar al-Islam.
The crusader states were small and short-lived.

Merchants and Sufi teachers adapting the faith to local customs
Turkic rulers defending Sunni Islam
The weakening of the Abbasid caliphs
questions.explanation: The source says Islam was carried “less by armies than by merchants and Sufi teachers.”
choiceExplanations: The Mongol attack was military and was not a spread of Islam.
Defending Sunni Islam describes politics, not peaceful spread.
The caliphs' decline is a political change, not a means of spread.

Mongol khans ruling in China
questions.explanation: The Delhi Sultanate was a Muslim state in northern India, where most subjects were Hindu.

the rejection of all non-Islamic knowledge

the closing of cities after the Mongol conquest

choiceExplanations: Trade continued and helped move ideas.
They drew on non-Islamic learning rather than rejecting it.
Scholars worked in cities from Cairo to Samarkand.

a trade route linking the Andes to the Valley of Mexico
a religious festival held each year
a tax paid in gold to the emperor
questions.explanation: The source defines the mit'a as “a set period of labor service on roads, terraces, and in the army.”
choiceExplanations: The mit'a was not a route; the roads linked the Inca Empire.
The mit'a was a labor obligation, not a festival.
The Inca collected labor rather than gold taxes.

choices: were Christian kingdoms that traded with Europe
depended on tribute from conquered city-states
grew powerful by controlling key resources: labor for the Inca and trade goods for Mali
governed through bureaucracies of officials trained for and selected by written examinations
questions.explanation: The Inca drew on labor service; Mali taxed gold and salt. Each controlled a resource that sustained the state.
choiceExplanations: Neither state was Christian.
Tribute from city-states describes the Mexica.

Sufism, which spread Islam into West Africa
Confucianism, which shaped government and social order in China
questions.explanation: Like the Church in Europe, Confucian ideas shaped East Asian government, education, and family life.
choiceExplanations: The Delhi Sultanate's rulers were Muslim.

questions.prompt: Which development described in Source D would most likely weaken the manorial system?
choices: The granting of land to vassals for military service.
Labor shortages after the Black Death strengthened peasants' bargaining power.
The spread of Church courts into every region.
The growth of stronger royal governments in England and France during the period.
questions.explanation: With perhaps a third of the population dead, surviving peasants were scarce and could demand better terms, loosening serfdom.
choiceExplanations: Granting land for service is part of the feudal system itself.
Church courts did not change peasants' labor.
Stronger monarchies developed alongside manorialism, not against it.
